title: A presidential election is about finding PMF for the candidate; if the product is bad, no one can save it
dek: A campaign is the fastest-scaling organization in a short window, but the product — the candidate — is already fixed. All you can do is product-market fit that product to the whole country's environment.
why: It breaks a campaign into product, field organizing, fundraising and polling systems, and the mapping to tech startups is concrete; the second half on Silicon Valley's turn to Trump is worth hearing.
who: Founders and investors interested in the politics-business analogy, especially those who want to see how campaign field organizing and media strategy map onto tech company growth and government relations.
skip: The opening self-introduction and the few minutes on the share of Chinese Americans in politics can be skipped.

points.h: A campaign is the fastest-scaling organization in a short window
points.body: Kevin directly analogizes a campaign to a tech startup: in 2007 Obama was just one of seven or eight Democratic candidates, and the team had to hire people, rent offices and find volunteers in an extremely short time, scaling up field capacity. The core job of a field organizer is not to make calls to canvass votes themselves, but to develop local volunteers, train them, and multiply the whole capacity. He specifically notes this playbook is very similar to the BD teams and station-chief systems at Didi and Meituan when they were fighting — pushing an app and pushing a candidate are the same underlying motion.

points.h: A campaign is easy to manage because there is only one goal: win
points.body: Kevin says a campaign is "both hard and not hard." Hard because the processes are immature and for the vast majority of people, doing it for more than two years makes you a veteran; not hard because the goal is extremely aligned — a company will want to do this product one moment and that product the next, it has to pivot, but in a campaign framework you just win, there is no other purpose. Strategy can change, but the product is already fixed, it is your candidate, and all that is left is how to product-market fit that product to the whole country's environment.

points.h: The first step in field organizing is grabbing voter registration, not votes
points.body: Kevin lays out the specific tactics: in the US you must register before voting, and when you register you can choose Democratic, Republican or independent, so the team's strategy is first to find local people and get them registered as Democratic voters, expanding the pool of people you can influence, and then canvass vote by vote. The second move is to push key states to lengthen and expand early voting options, because working-class people cannot take a day off on election day and queues take four or five hours, so giving more voting windows brings in the people you want to pull in. This voter registration plus early voting playbook was also used by Trump's team this year.

points.h: If the candidate product is bad, no team can save it
points.body: Kevin says the key to winning is first that the product has to be good — the candidate himself has to be a product worth pushing to society, and that is very hard to change. Obama's early debate level was average, he talked too much and explained in too much detail, and only later did he develop delivery and storytelling, but the product's foundation was good to begin with. Beyond a good product, a bad team also will not do, you need both. He also points out the difference from a startup: a company has no finish line and can go on forever, a campaign has a very clear finish line, which is whether you win on election day.

points.h: Trump's win was within expectations, just too fast and too stark
points.body: Kevin says this result was absolutely within his expectations, the only thing beyond expectations was the margin of victory and the speed of the result — he had judged it might drag on for a week or two, with disputes at polling places in swing states and lawyers from both sides litigating. He attributes the cause to a parallel with 2008: economic problems, the public lowering its expectations for personal and family economic prospects, inflation and the wealth gap, plus Trump being the "no-war candidate" while the US is heavily invested in both Ukraine and Israel, and the public mood is "why spend so much abroad and not take care of things at home."

points.h: Harris's team not embracing podcasts was a strategic loss
points.body: Kevin thinks the Democrats were still stuck in the old-school playbook on media strategy this time. Podcasts are already very mainstream in the US; a host like Joe Rogan, who comes from stand-up comedy, has no fixed political leaning, and does two- or three-hour episodes, represents a lot of ordinary Americans, and the long format actually builds trust; traditional cable TV is at most twenty-some minutes and has ads, and public trust in traditional media is at a historic low. Trump went on Joe Rogan and talked for three hours, and also did the 45-minute Lex Fridman episode; Harris's team did not embrace this channel well.

points.h: It is the Republican Party following Trump, not the other way around
points.body: Kevin says Trump himself is not a product produced by a party, he is the product, and everyone is adapting to follow him. He used to be a Democrat, and only borrowed the Republican framework and party processes to become the official candidate; if the Democratic mechanism could have worked, he could have gone that route too. Ideologically he is generally more aligned with traditional Republican views, but he has also overturned the Republican Party's core creed — the Republican tradition champions free markets, free trade and no tariffs, while he started adding tariffs in his first term and may add a lot more in his second.

points.h: Trump's biggest promise to tech is deregulation
points.body: Kevin says the market has high expectations for Trump's positive impact on US tech development, and the core promise is reducing regulations. The best example is energy, and energy is tied to AI development: building new power plants in the US, especially nuclear plants, is very difficult, blocked by all kinds of rules and regulations, and developing AI infrastructure requires a lot of energy, so he says he wants to cut many regulations so people can build infrastructure faster to feed tech development. Another is embracing crypto and web3. The risk is uncertainty — he may want to do something today and drop it tomorrow, while companies care more about stability, and "the government doing nothing is actually the best."

terms.def: The state where a product matches market demand well enough to grow organically; here it means the match between the candidate and the country's environment.
In the US you must register before voting, and when registering you can choose a party affiliation; it is the first step in field organizing to grab turf.
Voting windows opened before election day; the length and number of polling places vary by state.

I think first your product has to be good, the candidate has to be good — though the definition may be very fuzzy, it's something you can see when you see it.
